How to approve vacation requests fairly when everyone wants the same week

Every summer the same thing happens on a small team: three people ask for the second and third weeks of July, the rota only works with two of the five in the kitchen, and whoever the manager answers first gets the week. The decision feels personal because it is made one email at a time. Making it once, against written rules, with all the requests in front of you, is fairer and usually approves more of them.

Open the free planner

The method

1. Write down minimum cover per role, not per team

"We need two cooks and one cashier on every working day" is a rule you can check. "We can't have too many people off" is not. Count by role, because a team of nine can still be one sick day from having nobody who can run the till.

2. Decide the tie-break before you read the requests

Seniority, first to ask, who missed out last year, or a mix. Turn it into a number from 1 to 5 per request and write the rule down where people can see it. A rule chosen after you have seen who asked for what is not a rule.

3. Look at all requests together

The requests that clash are rarely the pairs you notice. A long trip in week two can block a short one in week three that overlaps by a single day. Check every working day against the minimums, and treat days nobody works as free.

4. Approve the best set, not the first fit

Going in the order the emails arrived is simple, and it is not always best: one early three-week request can block three people who each wanted four days. Compare the set that maximises priority with the first-come set and see what the shortcut would have cost.

5. Give a reason and a way forward to everyone else

"No" is easier to accept as "Tuesday the 15th is the day we drop to one cook; the 20th to the 24th works". Name the day that breaks the rule and offer the nearest dates that fit.

A worked example

An invented café has four baristas, three cooks and two cashiers, minimums of two, two and one, and eleven requests across July and early August. Approving in the order the requests arrived says yes to seven, but they are mostly low-priority long trips. The planner approves seven too, and every one of them is a higher-priority request: the priority score goes from 16 to 20, and two baristas who asked for a week each get it instead of two long low-priority trips. For each of the four it cannot approve, it names the first day that breaks a minimum and who is already off that day, for example Ana's request clashes on Wednesday 15 July because two of the four baristas are already off. It also suggests the nearest dates that fit.

Try it with your own team

Questions

Should vacation requests be approved first come, first served or by seniority?

Either can be fair if it is written down before the busy season and applied the same way to everyone. The cost of first come, first served is that an early request for a long stretch can block several shorter ones in the same weeks. Whatever rule you use, decide it first, then enter it as the priority column and let the arithmetic check the cover.

How many people can be off at once?

As many as leave the minimum on duty for every role on every working day. Four baristas with a minimum of two on duty means two can be off at the same time, not three. Check each role separately, because a team can have plenty of people overall and still have only one person who can do a given job.

Do weekends and days off count against cover?

Only days the person would otherwise work do. A request that spans a weekend nobody works uses cover for the weekdays only, and a request that falls entirely on days off never affects cover. Set the working days to match your rota if you open on weekends.

TIME-OFF REQUEST PLANNER · RUNS IN YOUR BROWSER · NOTHING UPLOADED

Too many people want the same week off? Settle it in a minute.

Paste your team with their roles and the time-off requests you have, say how many of each role must be on duty, and the tool picks the set of requests to approve that never drops a role below its minimum on any working day. Each request it cannot approve comes back with the day it clashes, who is already off and the nearest dates that would work. See what first come, first served would have cost you, and download the decisions as a CSV.

Your team list never leaves this browser tab. Planning aid, not legal, tax, or financial advice. It does not know your leave law, contract or balances. See how to approve vacation requests fairly for the method.

Your team

Requests

Dates look like 2026-07-06 or 7/6/2026. Both ends are days off. Put your own policy (seniority, who asked first, who had the last holiday) into the priority column. Lines starting with # are ignored.

How it is calculated

Hard rules (never broken): on every working day, the people on duty in each role stay at or above the minimum you gave (so at most headcount − minimum can be off); the total off on one day stays at or under your cap; nobody is approved off on a blackout date; one person is never counted off twice on the same day. Days outside the working days you listed never use cover. Objective: maximise the sum over approved requests of priority (times working days off, if you chose days), with ties going to more approvals and then to the request listed first. Search: an exact branch-and-bound over every combination of requests, started from the first-come, first-served answer and pruned by the best possible remaining weight, so on the sizes this page accepts the plan is the best for the rule you chose. If a very large set hits the search limit the page says so. The tests compare it with a brute-force search of every subset on random problems.

Not modelled: statutory or contractual leave rights, notice periods, accrued balances and carry-over, sick leave, part-time and shift patterns inside a working day, skills beyond a single role per person, and people who can cover two roles. Unverified: checked against exhaustive search and invented data in unit tests, not against a real workplace's policy or a leave law.

Common questions

How do I decide which vacation requests to approve when too many people ask for the same week?

List each request with its dates and how much it matters, say how many people each role needs on duty, and approve the set that never drops a role below that number on any working day. Do it by priority first, then by how many requests or days off you can say yes to. This tool searches every combination and shows the plan, and for each request it cannot approve, the day it breaks the rule and who is already off.

Is first come, first served the fairest way to approve time off?

It is simple and easy to defend, but it can be wasteful: one early request for three weeks can block three people who each wanted a few days in the same stretch. The planner shows what first come, first served would approve next to the best plan so you can see what the rule costs, and then you choose the rule you want to run by.

How does the planner choose between requests that cannot all be approved?

Every request has a priority from 1 to 5 (3 if you leave it blank). The plan maximises priority-weighted requests, or priority-weighted days off if you pick that, and breaks ties toward more approvals and then toward the request listed first. It is an exact search, so on up to about forty competing requests it is proven best for the rule you chose. Put your own seniority or first-come order into the priority column if that is your policy.

What counts as minimum cover?

For each role you give the least number of people who must be at work on every working day. If you have four baristas and need two on duty, at most two can be off at once. You can also cap the total number of people off per day across the whole team, and mark blackout dates such as a holiday weekend or stocktake when nobody is off.

What if a request is denied?

The tool gives the first working day that breaks the cover rule, names the approved people already off that day, and suggests the nearest window of the same length, up to six weeks either side, that would fit the approved plan. That turns a flat no into an offer of different dates.

Does this follow my local leave law or contract?

No. It does not know statutory leave, notice periods, accrual balances, carry-over, unpaid leave rules, union agreements or any rule about who must be granted leave. It only checks the cover rules you type in. Check the plan against the rules that apply to you before telling anyone.

Is my team list uploaded anywhere?

No. Names, roles and dates are read and solved in this browser tab. Nothing is sent to a server, there are no accounts or cookies, and the tool does not store your plan. It works offline once the page has loaded.
